channel.title: Video-Generation on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Video-Generation on Best of AI

item.title: FLUX 3
item.description: FLUX 3 is Black Forest Labs’ first model to train images, video, and audio together in a single architecture instead of stitching separate generators behind one interface. From a single prompt it can produce a still image or a combined video-and-audio clip up to 20 seconds long, and the same underlying approach, which the company calls Self-Flow, extends to robotic vision and action prediction. It launched July 23, 2026 in a limited release rather than a full public rollout, continuing FLUX’s role powering generative features inside tools like Adobe Photoshop and Picsart. Pricing and access remain narrower than the rest of the FLUX line at launch, with Black Forest Labs prioritizing existing API and platform partners before opening it more broadly.

item.title: Runway Gen-5
item.description:
Runway Gen-5 is the follow-up to Gen-4, extending maximum clip length and giving directors finer camera control: pans, tilts, and focus pulls specified as explicit parameters rather than left for the model to infer from a text prompt. Like its predecessors it takes text and image input and outputs video, available through Runway’s own app and API rather than as open weights.

Runway has kept pace with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora releases by shipping frequently and leaning into workflow features (multi-shot consistency, motion brushes, camera controls) that professional editors ask for, rather than only chasing raw fidelity. Gen-5 continues that pattern, with Runway pitching it primarily at studios and ad agencies already using Gen-4 in production pipelines rather than at hobbyist creators.

item.title: Act-One
item.description: Act-One is a feature inside Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha video model, released in October 2024, that turns an ordinary video of a person’s face into a driving signal for an AI-generated character. A creator films themselves on a phone or webcam, and Act-One maps their expressions, eye-lines, and timing onto a separate generated character without any motion-capture rig, facial markers, or manual keyframing. It supports multiple camera angles and can retarget a performance onto characters with different proportions from the original actor.

item.title: CogVideoX
item.description: CogVideoX is Zhipu AI’s open-weight text-to-video model, built with Tsinghua University’s KEG lab and released in August 2024 as a successor to the original CogVideo project. It ships in 2B and 5B parameter variants using a 3D causal VAE for spatial and temporal compression alongside an expert adaptive LayerNorm transformer, and it supports text-to-video, image-to-video, and video continuation from a single frame or prompt. The 5B model generates clips up to 10 seconds long at up to 768p resolution and 16 frames per second, and Zhipu later shipped a CogVideoX-1.5 update in November 2024 with longer, higher-resolution output. Weights are released under Apache 2.0 and hosted on Hugging Face, and Zhipu also serves the models through its own API, so CogVideoX works both as a self-hosted open model and as a hosted service, similar to how Stability AI and Runway position their video generators.

item.title: Emu Video
item.description: Emu Video is a text-to-video research model Meta introduced in November 2023, built on top of Meta’s Emu image generator. Rather than generating video directly from a text prompt in one step, it splits the job in two: first it uses Emu to generate a still image from the prompt, then it generates a video conditioned on both the text and that image. Meta reported that this factored approach let it skip the deep cascade of separate models that earlier systems like Google’s Imagen Video and Meta’s own Make-A-Video relied on, while still producing higher-resolution output. In human preference evaluations, Meta said raters favored Emu Video’s clips over Imagen Video’s and Make-A-Video’s the large majority of the time. It was released as a research paper and demo rather than a public product, and its techniques fed into later Meta video features rather than shipping as a standalone model.

item.title: Firefly Video
item.description: Firefly Video is Adobe’s text-to-video and image-to-video model, announced at Adobe MAX in October 2024 and opened to public beta through the standalone Firefly web app in February 2025. Adobe positions it as the first widely available video model built to be commercially safe, trained on licensed and public domain sources so businesses can use its output without copyright exposure. Inside Premiere Pro, it powers Generative Extend, a feature editors use to stretch a clip to cover a gap in footage, smooth a jump cut, or hold a shot longer without reshooting. Through 2025, Adobe added camera motion controls, start-frame image uploads, and prompt-based editing of existing footage, moving the tool from pure generation toward directed video editing. It remains in beta as of mid-2026, with Adobe rolling out updates alongside its other Firefly models rather than shipping a single finished version.

item.title: Hunyuan Video
item.description: HunyuanVideo is Tencent’s open-weight video generation model, released in December 2024 with roughly 13 billion parameters, which made it the largest open video model available at the time. It generates text-to-video and image-to-video clips up to about 720p and five seconds long, with prompt adherence and motion quality that reviewers compared favorably to closed models like Runway Gen-3 and Kling. Tencent released the full training and inference code along with pretrained weights on GitHub and Hugging Face under a license that permits commercial use in most jurisdictions, which was unusual for a model of this scale at release. The open weights let researchers and studios fine-tune it for specific styles or subjects rather than working only through an API. Tencent later followed up with HunyuanVideo-1.5, a smaller 8.3B-parameter model that reaches comparable quality with less compute.

item.title: Kling 2.0
item.description: Kling 2.0 is Kuaishou’s video generation model, launched in April 2025 at the company’s “Inspiration Comes True” event alongside a matching image model, Ketu 2.0. It takes text prompts or reference images and turns them into video, and Kuaishou focused the upgrade on smoother, more natural motion after earlier Kling versions drew criticism for stiff or jerky animation. The Master Edition adds a multimodal video editing feature that lets users add, remove, or replace elements in an existing generated clip by feeding in new text or images, rather than starting a generation over from scratch. Kuaishou positions Kling as a direct competitor to Runway, Pika, and Sora, and the 2.0 release was aimed at closing the gap on complex prompts, camera movement, and visual consistency across a shot. Kuaishou has continued iterating quickly since, with 2.1, 2.6, and 3.0 following within about a year.

item.title: Luma Dream Machine 1.0
item.description: Luma Dream Machine 1.0 is Luma AI’s first publicly available video generation model, launched in June 2024 as a free web tool that turns text prompts or a starting image into short video clips. It generates roughly five-second shots and was notable at launch for handling physics and motion more convincingly than most competing video models at the time, keeping characters and objects consistent as they move rather than warping between frames. Luma built it as a large-scale generative transformer trained directly on video and text, distinct from the diffusion-based approaches several rivals used. The tool grew quickly after launch, reportedly passing 25 million registered users, and it made Luma one of the more visible names in AI video generation alongside Runway and Pika.

item.title: Luma Ray 3
item.description: Luma Ray 3 is Luma AI’s flagship video generation model, released in September 2025 as what the company calls the first reasoning video model. Rather than generating pixels directly from a prompt, Ray 3 produces both text and visual tokens as it works, planning a scene and checking its own output before finalizing a clip, similar to a director sketching a storyboard before shooting. It is also the first video model to output true 10, 12, and 16-bit HDR footage in ACES2065-1 EXR format, aimed at professional film and advertising pipelines rather than just social clips. A Draft Mode lets users generate many quick low-cost variations before committing to a final high-resolution HDR render, and Adobe added Ray 3 to Firefly shortly after launch, giving it a route into mainstream creative software.
